Trustworthy Evaluation of AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Stable Diffusion Inpainting

Evaluation status: fully_evaluated. This report summarizes validated Notebook 09–30 evidence and creates no new scientific evidence.

Executive Summary

This standalone report evaluates Stable Diffusion Inpainting using validated restoration, metric, robustness, uncertainty, failure, explanation, and compute evidence.

What the evidence shows

  • Evaluation status: fully_evaluated.
  • Coverage: 300 paintings, 2620 cases and 8520 candidates.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting ranked fourth among the four full-scope methods under the approved family-balanced evaluation.
Limitation: Visual plausibility is not equivalent to historical or restoration trustworthiness. Better or worse metric-defined outcomes do not establish historical correctness. Any unsupported implication remains inconclusive.

1. Method Identity

This section defines what the evaluated method is, what role it can reasonably serve, and where that role ends.

Field Value
Model family Prompt Conditioned Latent Diffusion Inpainting
Methodological role Prompt Conditioned Stochastic Inpainting Baseline
Implementation Diffusers StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline
Model identifier stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-inpainting
Deterministic False
Prompt dependent True
Execution device cuda
Precision float16

Intended uses

  • prompt-conditioned generative inpainting baseline
  • repeated-seed variability analysis
  • controlled prompt-sensitivity analysis for thin scratches

Excluded uses

  • historically verified reconstruction
  • calibrated confidence estimation
  • unreviewed conservation decisions
Thesis alignment: RQ3: establishes the method's role inside a human-centred workflow.

What the evidence shows

  • Methodological role: prompt conditioned stochastic inpainting baseline.
  • Strengths: prompt-conditioned generative completion; seed-controllable stochastic candidates; supports empirical variability analysis.
  • Weaknesses: high hallucination and prompt-sensitivity risk; higher compute and candidate multiplier; thin-mask geometry can remain visible after compositing.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting should be interpreted within its declared methodological role rather than as an autonomous restoration authority.
Limitation: Visual plausibility is not equivalent to historical or restoration trustworthiness. Better or worse metric-defined outcomes do not establish historical correctness. Any unsupported implication remains inconclusive.

3. Overall Quality Evidence

Eleven transparent quality anchors combine classical, perceptual, feature, spatial, local, semantic, and structural evidence. Lower plotted rank is better.

Thesis alignment: RQ1: compares restoration quality using complementary evidence.

What the evidence shows

  • First-place transparent quality anchors: 0 of 11.
  • Family-balanced baseline rank: 4 of four full-scope methods.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting ranked fourth among the four full-scope methods under the approved family-balanced evaluation.
Limitation: Visual plausibility is not equivalent to historical or restoration trustworthiness. Better or worse metric-defined outcomes do not establish historical correctness. Any unsupported implication remains inconclusive.

4. Damage Types and Experiments

This section keeps damage-size sensitivity, mask robustness, and synthetic-degradation evidence separate. Positive adverse slopes indicate worse restoration behaviour under the stated exposure.

Thesis alignment: RQ2: evaluates damage size, mask geometry and synthetic degradation.

What the evidence shows

  • Damage-size deterioration was supported on 7 of 11 anchors.
  • 4 of 11 intervals crossed zero and remain inconclusive.
  • The focused damage-size, mask and degradation cohorts contain 35 paintings balanced across the five visual categories.
Conclusion: Larger damage made Stable Diffusion Inpainting worse on 7 anchors whose intervals remained above zero. Other anchors remain inconclusive.
Limitation: Focused experiments use controlled 35-painting cohorts. Metric-native slope magnitudes are not directly interchangeable.

5. Texture, Colour, and Seam Behaviour

Local texture, colour, and seam diagnostics test whether a plausible-looking repair remains visibly inconsistent near or inside the restored region.

Thesis alignment: RQ1: evaluates localized defects missed by global similarity.

What the evidence shows

  • First-place local anchors: 0 of three.
  • The anchors cover texture error, masked colour difference and boundary-seam mismatch.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting ranked first on 0 of the three local evidence anchors.
Limitation: Texture, colour and seam measurements represent different failure modes and use different scales.

6. Semantic and Structural Evidence

Semantic and structural measurements test local content and organization beyond pixel similarity. They remain proxies rather than proof of historical meaning.

Thesis alignment: RQ1 and the semantic/XAI extension: evaluates local structure and feature agreement.

What the evidence shows

  • First-place semantic or structural anchors: 0 of three.
  • Evidence covers local DINO similarity, structural affinity and structural SSIM.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting ranked first on 0 of the three semantic and structural anchors.
Limitation: Feature agreement does not establish iconographic correctness, artist intent or historical truth.

7. Uncertainty, Prompt, and Stability Evidence

Uncertainty is treated as empirical repeated-seed variability only. Deterministic methods and insufficient seed coverage are reported as not applicable.

Thesis alignment: RQ2: distinguishes stochastic sensitivity from restoration quality.

What the evidence shows

  • 1025 complete four-seed uncertainty groups were retained.
  • These comprise 780 canonical prompt-specific groups and 245 damage-size groups.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion supports empirical repeated-seed disagreement analysis. Lower disagreement may indicate greater stability, but does not prove correctness.
Limitation: Empirical disagreement is not calibrated confidence and does not measure historical correctness.

What the evidence shows

  • Observed mean runtime: 8.420 seconds per candidate.
  • Observed p95 runtime: 9.476 seconds.

Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting was slower than the fastest evaluated method. This is a compute disadvantage, not a quality conclusion.

12. Decision Support

Strengths

  • prompt-conditioned generative completion
  • seed-controllable stochastic candidates
  • supports empirical variability analysis

Weaknesses

  • high hallucination and prompt-sensitivity risk
  • higher compute and candidate multiplier
  • thin-mask geometry can remain visible after compositing
Thesis alignment: RQ3: translates evidence into bounded human-review support.

What the evidence shows

  • Intended uses: prompt-conditioned generative inpainting baseline; repeated-seed variability analysis; controlled prompt-sensitivity analysis for thin scratches.
  • Main strengths: prompt-conditioned generative completion; seed-controllable stochastic candidates; supports empirical variability analysis.
  • Main weaknesses: high hallucination and prompt-sensitivity risk; higher compute and candidate multiplier; thin-mask geometry can remain visible after compositing.
Conclusion: Stable Diffusion Inpainting is best used within its declared role and with comparison against references, diagnostics, flags and human judgement.
Limitation: The report supports prioritization and inspection; it does not authorize physical conservation treatment.

13. Limitations

The limitations below are retained from the canonical model card and evidence contract.

  • Runtime and memory observations describe one recorded local workstation and software environment.
  • The controlled 300-painting values are executed observations; only the explicitly labelled 600-painting and full-design SDXL values are projections.
  • Projected storage covers notebook-owned output artifacts and excludes model caches, environments, Git history, and downstream metric outputs.
  • SDXL scheduled 35 bounded cases across 30 paintings; 24 completed, one timed out and ten were skipped under the declared budget, so it cannot support a full-scope ranking.
  • LaMa per-case runtime includes transparent allocation from IOPaint batch wall-clock measurements.
  • Quality-anchor wins are descriptive validated Notebook 21 evidence, not a universal quality or conservation score.
  • Stable Diffusion produces plausible prompt-conditioned inpainting, not historically verified reconstruction.
  • The generic primary prompt and fixed inference settings are intentionally not tuned per painting or damage case.
  • Contextual prompts form a controlled ablation and are not used to select primary candidates.
  • Repeated seeds characterize stochastic sensitivity for a fixed predeclared subset and are not metric-selected.
  • Eligible synthetic-degradation cases are supplementary masked-removal diagnostics and remain separate from missing-content claims.
  • CUDA inference may not be byte-identical across hardware or software stacks; the complete environment is recorded.
  • The safety checker is disabled for this fixed research dataset and that policy is explicitly recorded.
  • The scratch-aware prompt is a controlled semantic-conditioning treatment and does not change the model, mask, seed, scheduler, inference resolution, compositing policy, or any other generation setting.
  • Thin scratch masks can lose or fragment spatial support during 512-pixel and latent-grid downsampling; prompting cannot be assumed to resolve that geometric limitation.
  • Literal scratch terminology is concentrated in the negative prompt because text encoders may not reliably interpret negation in positive prompts.
  • The 1,200 painting-seed pairs are repeated observations nested within 300 paintings; downstream inference must not treat all seed-level pairs as independent paintings.
Thesis alignment: RQ1, RQ2 and RQ3: defines what the evaluation does and does not establish.

What the evidence shows

  • Excluded uses: historically verified reconstruction; calibrated confidence estimation; unreviewed conservation decisions.
  • 17 persisted limitations are retained from the model card.
Conclusion: The evidence identifies comparatively better and worse metric-defined behaviour. Historical authenticity and physical conservation suitability remain inconclusive.
Limitation: Visual plausibility is not equivalent to historical or restoration trustworthiness. Better or worse metric-defined outcomes do not establish historical correctness. Any unsupported implication remains inconclusive.
